title: The first cities
summary: An urban way of life developed in southern Mesopotamia starting in the 4th millennium BCE. Uruk, Ur, Nippur and Lagash were among the places where, for the first time in human history, large numbers of people came to live together in cities. They grew in the marshy delta of the Tigris and Euphrates, and depended on exchange with the highlands for metals, timber and stone.

uncertainty.note: The transition from agrarian villages to major urban settlements in southern Mesopotamia unfolded across the Uruk period, conventionally dated throughout the fourth millennium BCE (c. 4000–3000 BCE).

as_recorded.value: between the 4th and the 3rd millennium BCE

where.modern_name: Uruk (Warka), Al-Muthanna Governorate, Iraq (primary urban center among southern Mesopotamian cities)
where.historical_name: Unug (Uruk), Sumer, southern Mesopotamia (marshland delta of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers)

importance.justification: The rise of the first cities marked the urban revolution in human history, inventing centralized administration, specialized labor, monumental architecture, and writing that defined subsequent civilized societies.
